understand.restatement: Combine intervals that overlap, including chains of overlaps, so the result covers exactly the same values without any overlapping intervals.
understand.outputs: A list of merged, non-overlapping intervals, returned in increasing start order.
constraints: Assume each interval satisfies start <= end.
Input may be unsorted or empty, and may contain duplicates or nested intervals.
The solution below does not mutate the input.
clarifying_questions: Do intervals that touch at an endpoint count as overlapping?
May I reorder or modify the input, and should the output be sorted?

examples.explanation: [1,3] overlaps [2,6]; the remaining intervals are separated by gaps.
After sorting, [2,2] is contained in [1,3], and [3,5] touches its endpoint.
An empty input has nothing to merge.

pattern.name: Intervals
pattern.why: Like arranging bridge spans by their starting markers, sorting intervals by start lets us extend the current merged span whenever the next interval overlaps.
pattern.recognize: Look for ranges, schedules, or segments that must be combined based on overlapping endpoints.

approach.brute_force: Copy the intervals, repeatedly search all pairs for an overlap, and replace any overlapping pair with its union. Restart after each merge; stop when no pair overlaps. Sort the final intervals for ordered output.
approach.brute_force_pseudocode:
work = copy(intervals)
repeat:
    find a pair a, b where max(a.start, b.start) <= min(a.end, b.end)
    if no such pair exists: break
    remove a and b
    add [min(a.start, b.start), max(a.end, b.end)]
return work sorted by start
approach.optimized: Sort a copy by start and use an output list to store merged intervals. For each interval, append a fresh pair if the list is empty or its start exceeds the last merged end. Otherwise, extend that last end to the maximum of both ends. Only the last output interval can overlap the next interval: all earlier output intervals end before the last one starts.

complexity.explanation: Sorting dominates the optimized solution; the subsequent scan visits each interval once. The sorted copy and output require linear space, including O(n) auxiliary space even when output is excluded. Repeated pair searching in the brute-force method has an O(n^3) worst-case upper bound: up to n merge rounds, each scanning O(n^2) pairs.
follow_ups: How would the solution change if the intervals were already sorted?

scenes.caption: Mira reaches a river workshop carrying four bridge plans: [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], and [15,18]. Each plan covers numbered river markers, including both ends. The mayor needs a clean map before the builders arrive, and Mira volunteers to untangle the crossings.

“Keep every covered marker, but stop drawing the same crossing twice,” says the mayor. Mira notices the first two plans share markers 2 and 3. Joining them should make one bridge from 1 to 6, while the distant crossings must remain separate.

At first, Mira compares every plan with every other plan, restarting whenever she joins two. The workshop clock ticks louder. “With a whole river of plans, I would keep checking the same crossings,” she groans, sliding the papers back across the table.

question.prompt: What makes Mira's first method slow?
options: It repeatedly searches pairs after merges.
question.hint: Think about how much work restarts after one successful merge.

scenes.caption: Then Mira lines the plans up by their starting markers. “Now I only need the last bridge on my clean map!” Since 2 is no greater than 3, she stretches [1,3] into [1,6]. The next start, 8, reveals a real gap.

question.prompt: What should Mira do with [8,10] after [1,6]?
question.hint: The next start is greater than the current end.

scenes.caption: By sunrise, Mira presents [1,6], [8,10], and [15,18], preserving every crossing without filling any gaps. Her coding solution uses an output list storing merged intervals: after sorting, efficient last-item checks, endpoint updates, and appends finish one forward scan. The builders cheer and unfold the map.

code_hotspots.why: Ordering intervals dominates the overall running time.
Each sorted interval is examined exactly once.
Each overlapping interval causes one constant-time endpoint update.

frames.note: Sort by start; this example is already in order.
The output is empty, so append a fresh [1,3] pair.
The interval overlaps, so extend the last end to max(3,6).
A gap separates the intervals, so append [8,10].
Append [15,18] after another gap and return the completed output.
